title: Determine Whether Matrix Can Be Obtained By Rotation
spaceBreakdown: - No additional containers are allocated; all work is done in place with index calculations.
approach:
Check the matrix against the target after 0°, 90°, 180°, and 270° rotations.  
A single rotation can be simulated by index mapping, so we only need to compare up to four times.  
If any rotated version matches, return true; otherwise return false.
hints:
Since n ≤ 10, you can afford to try every 90° rotation.  
Instead of physically rotating the matrix, compare elements using a formula that maps indices.

Use a simple index mapping: for a 90° clockwise rotation, element (i, j) moves to (j, n-1-i).  
For example, in a 2×2 matrix, (0,1) → (1,1).

**Single Element** - Only one cell, always matches after 0° rotation.  
`Input: mat=[[1]], target=[[1]]` → `Expected: true`  
⚠️ Bug: comparing only the first element and returning true → correct output, but fails if target differs.  

**All Zeros vs All Ones** - No rotation can change values.  
`Input: mat=[[0,0],[0,0]], target=[[1,1],[1,1]]` → `Expected: false`  
⚠️ Bug: using `==` instead of `!=` in the inner loop → returns true incorrectly.  

**Already Matched After 180°** - Must check all rotations, not just 90°.  
`Input: mat=[[1,0],[0,1]], target=[[1,0],[0,1]]` → `Expected: true`  
⚠️ Bug: stopping after first rotation check → returns false if 0° is not checked.

followUps.q: What if n could be up to 10⁵?
followUps.a: We would need an O(n²) algorithm to compare all rotations, which is infeasible. Instead, we could hash each rotation and compare hashes in O(n²) time but with O(n²) space, or use a more clever invariant.

followUps.q: How would you solve this if the matrix were not square?
followUps.a: For rectangular matrices, rotations change dimensions; we would need to compare against the appropriately transposed target for each rotation, increasing complexity to O(n·m).

followUps.q: Suppose we could only rotate the matrix in place without extra memory.
followUps.a: We would perform an in‑place 90° rotation algorithm (cyclically swapping elements) four times, each O(n²), and compare after each rotation, keeping space O(1).
